title: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes

subtopics.heading: What the OS does
subtopics.notes:
The OS is the link between hardware and applications.

Core responsibilities:
- File management (create / read / write / delete on storage)
- Application support: memory allocation, swap, process scheduling
- Input/output handling for keyboard, mouse, display, printer, etc.
- System management utilities to keep the OS healthy

Applications are written for a specific OS. An executable built for Windows will not run on Linux. Documents and media files are portable across OSes; executables are not.

Many modern applications are web-based, which makes them OS-independent at the user level (anything that runs Chrome can use them).
subtopics.whyOnExam: 1.1 is a frame-setting objective. The exam expects you to know that the OS sits between hardware and apps, why apps are OS-specific, and why web apps sidestep that.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing 'application portable across OS' (almost never) with 'document portable across OS' (almost always).

subtopics.heading: Workstation operating systems
subtopics.notes:
Four workstation OSes on the exam:

Windows
- Largest market share, broad industry support, many editions (10, 11, Server)
- Largest attack surface because of popularity
- Hardware compatibility depends on vendor-supplied drivers (quality varies)

Linux
- Free and open source, no licensing cost
- Distributed in many flavors (distributions); pick one that fits the use case
- Huge community support, no single 'Linux company' to call
- Newest hardware may lack drivers

macOS
- Runs exclusively on Apple hardware
- Tight hardware + software integration, designed with security in mind
- Smaller user base than Windows means less third-party industry support
- Higher initial hardware cost (Apple-only)

Chrome OS
- Built by Google, based on the Linux kernel
- Built around the Chrome browser; most apps run in the browser
- Minimal overhead, hardware from many manufacturers (mostly laptops)
- Heavy network dependency: lose connectivity, lose most apps
subtopics.whyOnExam: Expect questions framed as 'which OS fits scenario X' (cost, hardware lock-in, browser-only, etc.).
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking Linux because 'no cost' when the scenario also requires guaranteed vendor support. Linux has no central support vendor.

subtopics.heading: Mobile operating systems
subtopics.notes:
Three mobile OSes on the exam:

iPadOS
- Apple's iPad OS, separate from iOS
- Desktop-class Safari, second-monitor support via Sidecar, keyboard support, multitasking

iOS
- Apple's iPhone OS, closed source, Apple hardware only
- Apps must be built with Apple's Software Developer's Kit on macOS
- App Store requires Apple approval before publication

Android
- Open source, based on Linux
- Maintained by the Open Handset Alliance (consortium of companies)
- Runs on hardware from many manufacturers
- Apps developed on Windows, macOS, or Linux
- Distributed via Google Play and many third-party stores
subtopics.whyOnExam: Know which mobile OS is open vs closed source, and what hardware each runs on. Also know the developer pipeline (iOS requires macOS to develop; Android can be developed anywhere).
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming iOS and iPadOS are the same OS. They share design but are separate products. Sidecar is iPadOS-only.

subtopics.heading: Filesystem types
subtopics.notes:
Cross-platform readable (Windows / Linux / macOS):
- FAT32: legacy, 2 TB volume max, 4 GB file max
- NTFS: Windows default; modern Linux and macOS can read AND write
- exFAT: Microsoft's extended FAT; designed for flash drives; files larger than 4 GB; cross-platform

Windows-specific:
- NTFS: compression, file encryption, quotas, ACLs
- ReFS (Resilient File System): NTFS successor; self-healing, RAID-like features, large arrays; Server 2012+, limited desktop support; NOT widely deployed

Linux:
- ext4: standard Linux filesystem; also used in Android
- XFS: high-performance, large filesystem support, journaling, minimal fragmentation; used in data centers

Apple:
- APFS (Apple File System): macOS 10.12.4+, iOS, iPadOS; optimized for SSDs; encryption, snapshots, integrity checks
subtopics.whyOnExam: Memorize which filesystem goes with which OS by default. Pay attention to FAT32's 4 GB file limit and exFAT being the flash-drive answer.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking ReFS for a desktop scenario. ReFS is server-focused and not widely deployed on desktops. Default desktop answer is still NTFS.

subtopics.heading: Vendor life-cycle and compatibility
subtopics.notes:
End-of-life (EOL) varies by vendor. Apple's EOL policy differs from Microsoft's. Always check the vendor-specific support window.

Why it matters:
- EOL OS stops getting security patches
- EOL hardware may stop getting drivers

Compatibility across OSes:
- Data files (documents, spreadsheets, images, media): usually portable
- Executables: never portable across OS families
- Some software ships per-OS builds (e.g. an app with both Windows and macOS installers)
- Web-based apps sidestep the issue entirely
subtopics.whyOnExam: Expect a scenario asking what happens after EOL or why an .exe won't run on a Mac. The answer is usually 'rebuild as the right architecture' or 'use a web alternative'.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming EOL only means 'no new features'. The bigger issue is no more security patches.
